options.text: A plant that lives in water
A plant adapted to survive in dry conditions with limited water
A plant that only grows at night
A plant that lives in salty water

questions.explanation: Xerophytes are plants adapted to survive in hot, dry environments where water is scarce. They have evolved structural features to reduce water loss.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an adaptation of xerophytes to reduce water loss?

options.text: Many stomata on the upper surface
Thick waxy cuticle, sunken stomata, and rolled leaves
Large, thin leaves
No roots

questions.explanation: Xerophytes have adaptations such as thick waxy cuticles (reduces evaporation), sunken stomata (trap humid air), rolled leaves (reduce exposed surface area), and reduced leaf size or spines.

options.text: A plant adapted to live in or on water
A plant adapted to dry conditions
A plant that grows in deserts
A plant that lives underground

questions.explanation: Hydrophytes are plants that are adapted to living in water or waterlogged conditions. Examples include water lilies and pondweed.

questions.stem: How do cacti reduce water loss?

options.text: By having large leaves
By having leaves reduced to spines, a thick waxy cuticle, and storing water in fleshy stems
By closing their roots
By growing only in the shade

questions.explanation: Cacti have leaves reduced to spines (reducing surface area for transpiration), thick waxy stems for water storage, and a thick cuticle. Their photosynthesis occurs in the green stem.

questions.stem: Why do marram grass leaves roll up in dry conditions?

options.text: To trap moist air inside the rolled leaf, reducing the water potential gradient and slowing transpiration
To protect from herbivores
To increase photosynthesis
To absorb more light

questions.explanation: Rolling the leaf traps a layer of humid air near the stomata (which are on the inner surface), reducing the concentration gradient for water vapour and thus reducing the rate of transpiration.

options.text: Thick waterproof layers
Protective spines
Specialised roots for water absorption
Large air spaces in stems and leaves that provide buoyancy and allow gas transport

questions.explanation: Aerenchyma are large air spaces in the tissues of hydrophytes that provide buoyancy to keep leaves at the water surface for light and gas exchange, and allow oxygen to reach submerged roots.

questions.stem: Why do hydrophytes often have stomata on the upper surface of their leaves?

options.text: To release water into the air faster
Because the lower surface is in contact with water, so stomata on top allow gas exchange with the air
To absorb more water
Because the lower surface is more attractive to insects

questions.explanation: In floating hydrophytes, the lower leaf surface is in contact with water. Stomata are therefore on the upper surface so they can exchange gases (CO2 and O2) with the atmosphere.
